lesson.title: Reviewer Judgment Calibration
lesson.summary: Teach reviewers how experienced human reviewers think about hesitation, acceptance, rejection, borderline calls, severity, risk tolerance, contradiction, and confidence calibration.
learningObjectives: Recognize judgment profiles and how they shape reviewer behavior.
Explain why a reviewer hesitated, accepted, or rejected a case.
Distinguish true false positives from cautious rejections.
Distinguish true false negatives from overconfident acceptances.
Calibrate confidence, severity, and risk tolerance separately.
Preserve borderline decisions instead of collapsing them into certainty.

concepts.title: Judgment Profiles
concepts.summary: Reviewer behavior patterns that describe how a human reviewer tends to hesitate, accept, reject, or escalate.

concepts.title: False Positive Library
concepts.summary: Known cases where overcalling a finding would be a mistake.

concepts.title: False Negative Library
concepts.summary: Known cases where undercalling a finding would be a mistake.

concepts.title: Edge Cases
concepts.summary: Borderline situations that should not be flattened into simple yes or no decisions.

concepts.title: GCAM Interpretation Notes
concepts.summary: Notes that explain how judgment calibration affects GCAM interpretation and final mapping.

concepts.title: Human Reviewer Philosophy
concepts.summary: Principles that describe how experienced reviewers think about doubt, restraint, and responsibility.

concepts.title: Risk Tolerance
concepts.summary: How much uncertainty the reviewer will tolerate before escalating or rejecting.

concepts.title: Severity Calibration
concepts.summary: How the reviewer matches seriousness to the actual strength and scope of the evidence.

concepts.title: Confidence Calibration
concepts.summary: How confidence should rise or fall when the evidence becomes stronger, weaker, or contradictory.

concepts.title: Decision Confidence
concepts.summary: The final confidence attached to a reviewer decision after weighing support and contradiction.

concepts.title: Contradicting Evidence
concepts.summary: Evidence that pulls the reviewer away from an overly simple conclusion.

concepts.title: Supporting Evidence
concepts.summary: Evidence that legitimately supports the reviewer decision and should be cited explicitly.

concepts.title: Decision Uncertainty
concepts.summary: The degree of unresolved doubt that remains after review.

concepts.title: Decision Ambiguity
concepts.summary: Cases where more than one answer remains plausible.

concepts.title: Borderline Decisions
concepts.summary: Calls that sit at the boundary between accept, reject, and review.

reviewerQuestions.reasoningGuidance: Explain what was missing, contradictory, or borderline.
evidenceRequirements: Cite the evidence that caused hesitation.

reviewerQuestions.purpose: Why did the reviewer accept or reject?
reviewerQuestions.reasoningGuidance: Separate the outcome from the confidence level.
evidenceRequirements: Name the support or the missing support.

reviewerQuestions.purpose: Is this a false positive or false negative risk?
reviewerQuestions.reasoningGuidance: Use caution to distinguish overcalling from undercalling.
evidenceRequirements: Identify the risk direction and why it matters.

reviewerQuestions.reasoningGuidance: Keep severity and confidence separate unless the evidence clearly supports both.
evidenceRequirements: Explain whether severity and confidence move together.

reviewerQuestions.reasoningGuidance: Use review when the answer is not stable enough for a final call.

reviewerQuestions.purpose: What confidence curve should the reviewer use?
reviewerQuestions.reasoningGuidance: Show how confidence shifts as support, contradiction, and ambiguity change.

examples: The reviewer hesitates because the scene is borderline and the target cue is weak.
The reviewer accepts only after contradiction is resolved and the support is stable.
The reviewer rejects because the case looks like a false positive risk.
The reviewer keeps a weak case in review to avoid a false negative.
counterExamples: The reviewer forces certainty in a borderline case.
The reviewer treats a cautious rejection as a final finding.
The reviewer turns a weak clue into a strong conclusion.
The reviewer hides uncertainty instead of reporting it.

minimum: At least one explicit clue or one valid contextual clue must exist.
The reviewer must explain why hesitation remains if the case is borderline.
strong: Multiple clues point the same way.
Contradicting evidence has been checked and addressed.
weak: A plausible reading that remains unstable.
insufficient: A forced conclusion before contradiction is resolved.
confidenceGuidance: High confidence when the call is stable and corroborated.
Medium confidence when the call is plausible but still debated.
Low confidence when contradiction or ambiguity remains strong.
Review required when hesitation cannot be resolved.

conceptRelationships.note: Profiles are shaped by how a human reviewer thinks.
A reviewer must balance overcalling and undercalling.
Edge cases often become borderline decisions.
Support must be weighed against contradiction.
Confidence calibration produces the final confidence.
GCAM interpretation affects how severity is framed.

glossaryReferences.note: The answer is close enough to require reviewer caution.
Confidence should change with evidence quality.

False positive and false negative handling depend on evidence sufficiency.
Confidence calibration, severity calibration, and borderlines map here.

reportTemplates.reasonTemplate: Explain why the reviewer hesitated, accepted, rejected, or escalated, and how confidence changed with support and contradiction.
reportTemplates.recommendationTemplate: Preserve the calibration reasoning in the report instead of collapsing borderline calls.

metadata.subject: reviewer intelligence
falsePositiveLibrary: Borderline clue that should remain review.
falseNegativeLibrary: Weak-looking case that still deserves acceptance.
Under-called evidence that should have been escalated.
gcamInterpretationNotes: Confidence should follow the evidence, not the urgency of the decision.
Severity must be justified independently from certainty.
humanReviewerPhilosophy: Be cautious when the evidence is borderline.
riskTolerance: Low risk tolerance for uncertain findings.
Higher risk tolerance for clearly corroborated calls.
severityCalibration: Severity rises only when evidence and context are stable.
Severity should not be inflated by a weak signal.
decisionConfidence: Final confidence should reflect the resolved evidence state.
contradictingEvidence: Evidence that weakens the first reading.
supportingEvidence: Evidence that strengthens the chosen reading.
decisionUncertainty: Uncertainty remains when the evidence is incomplete.
decisionAmbiguity: Ambiguity exists when more than one reading survives.
borderlineDecisions: Cases near the boundary between accept, reject, and review.
decisionExamples: A reviewer hesitates because the case is borderline.
A reviewer accepts after contradiction is resolved.
A reviewer rejects a likely false positive.
decisionAntiPatterns: Forcing a final decision too early.
decisionExceptions: Documentary framing may change the outcome.
Historical narration may justify a different judgment.
